units.text:
What is Acceptance Sampling?
 Definition:
   Acceptance sampling is a statistical quality control
      technique used to determine whether to accept or
       reject a batch (lot) of products by inspecting only a
     sample of items, not the entire lot.
 Attribute vs. Variable Inspection:
    Attribute: Classifies each item as conforming or
     nonconforming (does not specify how much it
      deviates).
   Variable: Measures a numerical quality characteristic
       (e.g., weight, length, concentration).
 Acceptance sampling can be performed during inspection of
 incoming raw materials, components, and assemblies, in
 various phases of in-process operations, or during final
 product or service inspection.

units.text:
Purpose of Acceptance Sampling

Key Purpose:
   To decide whether to accept or reject a batch of products
   based on the inspection results from a sample rather than
  100% inspection.
Why Not Inspect Everything?
Destructive testing may make 100% inspection impossible.
Sampling saves time & resources.
Reduces inspection errors due to fatigue.

“Acceptance sampling can be performed during inspection
of incoming raw materials, components, and assemblies, in
various phases of in-process operations, or during final
product or service inspection.”

units.text:
Where is Acceptance Sampling Used?

  Common Applications:
 Incoming materials: Quality assurance for parts/raw
    materials.
  In-process inspection: Quality checks during
    manufacturing.
  Finished products: Final inspection before sale or
    shipment.
  Inter-organizational: Between companies and
    suppliers/vendors.
  Internal checks: Between departments or divisions
    within a company

Why is Acceptance Sampling
Relevant?

 Sampling doesn’t improve process quality—only
    decides batch acceptance.
  Quality must be designed and built into
    products/processes.
 Acceptance sampling helps monitor but cannot
    "inspect quality into" products.

Advantages and Disadvantages of
Sampling

 Advantages
 Essential where inspection is destructive
Economical and less handling damage
Reduces inspection errors (less fatigue)
 Motivates suppliers/processes to improve quality
 Disadvantages
Risk of accepting bad or rejecting good lots (risks)
Less information than 100% inspection
More planning/documentation than 100% inspection

units.text:
Producer’s Risk & Consumer’s Risk
 in Acceptance Sampling

Producer’s Risk (α):
The probability of rejecting a "good" lot, typically one with an
acceptable low level of nonconformance. This risk arises due to
the random nature of sampling.
  Goal: Minimize α to avoid unnecessary rejection of acceptable lots.

Consumer’s Risk (β):
The probability of accepting a "bad" lot, one with a high or
unacceptable level of nonconformance. This risk also stems
from sampling variation.
  Goal: Minimize β to protect the consumer from poor quality.

Operating Characteristic Curve
The Operating Characteristic (OC) curve is a graphical
 representation of the performance of a sampling plan.
Plots the probability of accepting a lot (Pa) (y-axis) against the
 proportion nonconforming (p) in the lot (x-axis).
Discriminatory Power:
  Shows how well a sampling plan can distinguish between “good”
  (low defect) and “bad” (high defect) lots.
Decision Rule:
  High Pa for good quality.
  Low Pa for poor quality.
Sampling Parameters Impact:
  Sample size (n), Acceptance number (c), Lot size (N) affect the
  curve shape.

The Ideal OC Curve (Conceptual)
Ideal Shape:
  Probability of acceptance (Pa) is 1 for all lots with defect
   proportion ≤ p₀ (all “good” lots accepted).
  Probability drops instantly to 0 for p > p₀ (all “bad” lots rejected).
Reality:
  Practical OC curves are not ideal—in practice, there's always a
   chance of accepting/rejecting due to sampling variation.
